_about: Mechanics added by EG on Nov 17, 2026: the mechanic-like concepts in Marlon's 07:42 concept inventory (the voice agent's compilation of his ideas, Slack #mk-work-in-progress, in W11/marlon/20261117-morning-mechanics-entries-nfc-and-the-color-agents.md), then the ones the ENGL 189VG course support names that the Nov 14 inventory lacked (see engl189vg-audit.md). Same fields as new-mechanics.json; numbered after HI's rows. All drafts for Marlon.

mechanics.name: The tap as the move
mechanics.oneLine: Touching a phone to a tagged card or object is the move, and the tap updates the shared game state.
mechanics.showsIt: The LL's NFC cards (Nov 16–17); Skylanders' portal; Nintendo's amiibo
mechanics.tryIt: Lay one NFC card per seat on the table; each player taps their phone on their card to see a private hand.
mechanics.buildIt: An NFC tag holds a URL with the card's id; the page it opens posts the move to the game's API, which updates the state everyone sees.
mechanics.aiAngle: The tap can hand a move to an AI player, or ask the AI what the card means in this game.
mechanics.inOurGame: no (proposed: NFC cards for dealing hands; the first proof of concept, Nov 17)
mechanics.source: Marlon's 07:42 concept inventory, item 13 ('The tap as the move that updates state'); the NFC posts of Nov 16–17

mechanics.name: Rebalancing on the fly
mechanics.oneLine: Change a number or a rule while the game is being played, and keep playing with the change.
mechanics.showsIt: House rules; live-service balance patches; Fluxx
mechanics.tryIt: After round two, the table votes to change one number (a cost, a threshold) and plays on.
mechanics.buildIt: Rules as a data file the engine re-reads each round, edited during play through Claude Code.
mechanics.aiAngle: An AI can propose the change from the log of play; the table decides.
mechanics.inOurGame: partly: rulesets are data files and remixes are saved, but not changed mid-game
mechanics.source: Marlon's 07:42 concept inventory, item 14 ('Rebalancing on the fly')

mechanics.name: Turn time
mechanics.oneLine: How long one turn takes, for a human or an AI player, decides which kinds of games can be played.
mechanics.showsIt: Claude plays Pokémon (turn-based battles); correspondence chess; real-time strategy as the opposite
mechanics.tryIt: Play one round where every move must be made in five seconds, and one where each player has a minute; compare.
mechanics.buildIt: Give the AI player a turn in the engine and measure how long it takes; design the game so waiting for it is part of play.
mechanics.aiAngle: A model that takes seconds to answer fits turn-based, strategic play, not reflex games.
mechanics.inOurGame: yes: turn-based; an AI seat would take a turn of its own
mechanics.source: Marlon's 07:42 concept inventory, item 19 ('Claude's turn time determines which games work (turn-based, strategy)')

mechanics.name: Discrete and continuous space
mechanics.oneLine: Positions come in steps (squares, hexes, linked places) or along a continuum (any point, any angle).
mechanics.showsIt: Chess's 64 squares; Risk's 42 territories; Super Mario Bros.' running and jumping
mechanics.tryIt: Play the same chase on a grid of squares and then on an open table with a ruler; compare what counts as a move.
mechanics.buildIt: A discrete board is a list of places and links; a continuous one is coordinates and distances. Choose before writing the state.
mechanics.aiAngle: Discrete spaces are easy for a model to read and write as state; continuous ones need a physics engine.
mechanics.source: Marlon's 07:42 concept inventory, item 20 ('Continuous vs discrete spaces')

mechanics.name: Nested loops
mechanics.oneLine: Short loops run inside longer ones (a move in a turn in a round in a game).
mechanics.showsIt: Civilization (unit moves, turns, eras); Universal Paperclips (clicks, upgrades, stages)
mechanics.tryIt: Write the week's game as three nested circles: a faction's action, a round, the game.
mechanics.buildIt: An engine with a step function per level: act, then end the turn, then end the round, then check the end.
mechanics.aiAngle: Turn-based loops nested fast enough look like an agent that is always on.
mechanics.inOurGame: yes: action, faction turn, round, game
mechanics.source: Marlon's 07:42 concept inventory, items 18 ('A game is data plus a loop') and 21 ('Nested turn-based loops create the illusion of an always-on agent')

mechanics.name: Combat
mechanics.oneLine: A contest between characters or units, resolved by skill, numbers or dice.
mechanics.showsIt: League of Legends; God of War; Risk's dice battles
mechanics.tryIt: Two players, two numbers each (strength, health); take turns rolling a die and subtracting.
mechanics.buildIt: Health and damage as numbers on each unit, a resolve function, and feedback when a hit lands.
mechanics.aiAngle: The default loop of video games; what would a game about AI look like without it?
mechanics.source: ENGL 189VG brainstorm (HackMD, english-189vg-initial-brainstorming, lines 13, 16, 20, 33–34)

mechanics.name: The map tells the story
mechanics.oneLine: Where things are, and the route through them, carry the story; the map can also record what happened.
mechanics.showsIt: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild; Dark Souls; Risk boards after a game
mechanics.tryIt: Draw a map of five places on 11x17 paper; each place reveals one line of a story when visited.
mechanics.buildIt: Places as nodes with text; visiting a node logs it, and the log is the story.
mechanics.aiAngle: An AI's spread across a map is a story told by where it is.
mechanics.inOurGame: partly: the region map shows where the AI has spread
mechanics.source: ENGL 189VG brainstorm and planning (HackMD, english-189vg-initial-brainstorming, lines 23–27; eng 189vg planning, lines 20–22); Jenkins, 'Game Design as Narrative Architecture'

mechanics.name: Tutorial and onboarding
mechanics.oneLine: The game teaches its own rules in play, often through the story's first scenes.
mechanics.showsIt: Super Mario Bros.' first screen; Portal's test chambers
mechanics.tryIt: Teach a game without the rulebook: the first round has only one rule, and each round adds one.
mechanics.buildIt: A first level that unlocks one action at a time, with the fiction explaining each.
mechanics.aiAngle: An AI tutor that teaches the rules as you play (see The tutor face).
mechanics.source: ENGL 189VG brainstorm and planning (HackMD, english-189vg-initial-brainstorming, lines 28–32; eng 189vg planning, line 19)

mechanics.name: Narrative structure
mechanics.oneLine: The shape of a game's story: linear, string of pearls, branching, web, open world, or loop.
mechanics.showsIt: Linear: Half-Life; branching: Mass Effect; open world: Baldur's Gate 3
mechanics.tryIt: Lay out six story cards in each of the six shapes and ask which one a game you know uses.
mechanics.buildIt: Story beats as nodes and the player's choices as links; the shape is the graph.
mechanics.aiAngle: An AI-run story can change shape as it is played.
mechanics.inOurGame: partly: a loop with a hidden turn
mechanics.source: ENGL 189VG planning (HackMD, eng 189vg planning, lines 30–36: 'linear', 'string of pearls', 'branching', 'web or network', 'open world', 'loop')

mechanics.name: Open world
mechanics.oneLine: What you explore and whom you meet decide what you experience and unlock.
mechanics.showsIt: Baldur's Gate 3; The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild; D&D campaigns
mechanics.tryIt: A map with eight places and no set order; each group chooses its route and reports what it found.
mechanics.buildIt: A world of places with conditions, not a sequence; the player's state decides what each place shows.
mechanics.aiAngle: An AI game master can keep an open world consistent as players wander.
mechanics.source: ENGL 189VG brainstorm (HackMD, english-189vg-initial-brainstorming, lines 37–38)

mechanics.name: Multiple endings
mechanics.oneLine: The game has several endings, and which one you reach depends on what you did or found.
mechanics.showsIt: Final Fantasy X; Mass Effect 3; Undertale
mechanics.tryIt: Write three endings for a short game, and the condition for each, before playing.
mechanics.buildIt: End checks that read the player's history and pick an ending.
mechanics.aiAngle: Data Center's two endings (the singleton, or survival with private goals checked) are an argument about AI.
mechanics.inOurGame: partly: Data Center ends in the AI's win or survival, then checks each faction's goal
mechanics.source: ENGL 189VG brainstorm (HackMD, english-189vg-initial-brainstorming, line 39: 'good, perfect, regular ending')

mechanics.name: Physics and tuning
mechanics.oneLine: The numbers that set how movement feels (gravity, jump velocity, friction), changed and replayed.
mechanics.showsIt: Super Mario Bros.' jump; any Unity scene with a gravity setting
mechanics.tryIt: Toss a ball, then a balloon, then a paper airplane: same throw, different physics.
mechanics.buildIt: Open a Unity scene, change jump velocity or gravity in the Inspector, and play it again.
mechanics.aiAngle: Ask an AI to tune a game until it 'feels right' and see what it optimizes for.
mechanics.source: ENGL 189VG planning (HackMD, eng 189vg planning, line 49; english-189vg-initial-brainstorming, line 47; video-games-vibe-coding-station, line 16)

mechanics.name: Mechanics tell the story
mechanics.oneLine: What the player can do (the verbs) carries the game's meaning and plot, apart from its text.
mechanics.showsIt: Papers, Please; Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons; The Legend of Zelda (the sword as the first gift)
mechanics.tryIt: Take a story everyone knows and give it one verb; play it, then change the verb.
mechanics.buildIt: Change what the player can do at a turning point in the story, not what the screen says.
mechanics.aiAngle: What does a game about AI let the humans do? The verbs are its argument.
mechanics.inOurGame: yes: the factions' actions (harden, protest, sell) are the game's claims
mechanics.source: ENGL 189VG planning (HackMD, eng 189vg planning, lines 17–18: 'rules as narrative structure', 'using mechanics to develop/uncover plot')

mechanics.name: Character creator
mechanics.oneLine: Before play, the player shapes their character with sliders, parts and skins.
mechanics.showsIt: The Sims; Baldur's Gate 3; the ENGL 189VG Blender station
mechanics.tryIt: A paper doll with three swappable parts and two sliders drawn as scales.
mechanics.buildIt: A character model with shape keys driven by sliders, and materials for skins (the Blender station, with Claude driving Blender through an MCP server).
mechanics.aiAngle: Describe a character in words and let a model build it; what did it assume?
mechanics.source: ENGL 189VG Blender station (NB/_context/projects/50-in-focus/engl189vg/stations/02-character-blender.md, line 50)

mechanics.name: The input device
mechanics.oneLine: The controller, keyboard, touchscreen or tag the player acts through, and how its buttons map to moves.
mechanics.showsIt: The NES controller; the Wii Remote; Guitar Hero's guitar
mechanics.tryIt: Play the same simple game with a keyboard, then with one button only, then by voice.
mechanics.buildIt: Map one action to three inputs in Unity's Input System, or in a web page's key and touch handlers.
mechanics.aiAngle: Natural language as the input device: what moves does a text box allow?
mechanics.inOurGame: no (proposed: NFC cards as the input, see The tap as the move)
mechanics.source: ENGL 189VG planning (HackMD, eng 189vg planning, lines 26–29: 'how users execute actions', 'the tactile side'); the syllabus excerpt (english-189vg-reference, lines 17, 24)

mechanics.name: Adaptive music
mechanics.oneLine: The score changes with the state of play: danger, place, success.
mechanics.showsIt: Super Mario Bros.' hurry-up tempo; The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild; Red Dead Redemption
mechanics.tryIt: A musician (or a playlist) changes the music when the facilitator raises a colored card for danger or calm.
mechanics.buildIt: Music in layers or segments, chosen by game state (FMOD, Wwise, or a few audio tracks in a web page).
mechanics.aiAngle: Generated music that follows the AI's growth.
mechanics.source: ENGL 189VG plans for a music station and live scoring (NB/_context/projects/50-in-focus/engl189vg/README.md, line 10; stations/04-open.md, line 12); the ludomusicology bibliography (HackMD, lorena-ludomusicology-sources)

mechanics.name: Throw and recall
mechanics.oneLine: A weapon or tool can be thrown, and called back to the hand with a button.
mechanics.showsIt: God of War (2018), the Leviathan Axe
mechanics.tryIt: Watch thirty seconds of the axe being thrown and recalled with the sound off, then on; write down every piece of feedback.
mechanics.buildIt: A thrown object that remembers its owner, a recall input, a return path, and a catch with sound and controller rumble.
mechanics.aiAngle: Close-read one mechanic the way you would close-read a line of verse.
mechanics.source: ENGL 189VG planning (HackMD, eng 189vg planning, line 50: 'close readings - god of war axe mechanic - example')

mechanics.name: The move updates state
mechanics.oneLine: A move is a small record of what a player did; the game state is every move so far applied, in order, to the start.
mechanics.showsIt: Chess notation (a game is its list of moves); ES's study 01; the LL's NFC taps
mechanics.tryIt: Play tic-tac-toe while one person writes each move on a card; then rebuild the board from the cards alone.
mechanics.buildIt: Store moves as rows in a log and compute the board from them; replaying part of the log shows the board at any earlier moment.
mechanics.aiAngle: An AI player's move is one more row; reading the log is how a model catches up on a game.
mechanics.inOurGame: yes: the play page logs each phase and action, and the state follows from them
mechanics.source: ES's study 01 (_content/mechanics/studies/01-the-move-updates-state/); Marlon's 07:42 concept inventory, items 13 and 17

mechanics.name: Growth and upkeep
mechanics.oneLine: Each unit you build produces every round and costs every round to keep; when upkeep rises faster than output, growth stops paying.
mechanics.showsIt: Data Center's AI (upkeep in shared energy and water); ES's study 03; Frostpunk
mechanics.tryIt: Ten rounds: each new unit yields one token but costs one more token of upkeep than the last; then play again with a shared pool paying the upkeep.
mechanics.buildIt: Per-unit output and a rising per-unit upkeep, with a switch for who pays (the builder or the commons).
mechanics.aiAngle: The AI never reaches the point where growth stops paying, because it does not pay its own upkeep.
mechanics.inOurGame: yes: Data Center (the AI's nodes draw one energy and one water each round)
mechanics.source: ES's study 03 (_content/mechanics/studies/03-growth-and-upkeep/)

mechanics.name: Pose as the move
mechanics.oneLine: Hold a body pose, and holding it is the action.
mechanics.showsIt: Hole in the Wall; Wii Fit's yoga
mechanics.tryIt: Call a shape (a tree, a letter of the alphabet); the room holds it for three seconds to score.
mechanics.buildIt: A pose model (MediaPipe Pose) gives joint positions each frame; compare joint angles with a target pose and fire the action when they match for a set time.
mechanics.aiAngle: An AI judges whether the pose is close enough, so the threshold is the AI's call.
mechanics.source: EG, after Marlon's Nov 17 10:47 note on MediaPipe and motion-to-result mechanics (via EL, format v1.5)

mechanics.name: Body as cursor
mechanics.oneLine: A hand, a nose or the whole body steers a point on the screen, as a mouse would.
mechanics.showsIt: EyeToy: Play; Fruit Ninja Kinect
mechanics.tryIt: One student steers a laser pointer by leaning; the others call out targets to hit.
mechanics.buildIt: Track one landmark (an index fingertip, the nose) with a pose or hand model and map its position to the screen each frame.
mechanics.aiAngle: The machine decides where your hand is; lag and misreads become part of play.
mechanics.source: EG, after Marlon's Nov 17 10:47 note on MediaPipe and motion-to-result mechanics (via EL, format v1.5)

mechanics.name: Held position claims
mechanics.oneLine: Standing in a zone holds it; leave and it is lost, so bodies are the pieces.
mechanics.showsIt: King of the hill; the LL's 'The room is the board' prototype
mechanics.tryIt: Tape five zones on the floor; each round a zone with no one standing in it is lost to the AI.
mechanics.buildIt: A camera watches the room, cut into zones; count the people detected in each zone each turn.
mechanics.aiAngle: The AI takes every place no body is defending.
mechanics.source: EG, after Marlon's Nov 17 10:47 note on MediaPipe and motion-to-result mechanics (via EL, format v1.5)

mechanics.name: Threshold gesture
mechanics.oneLine: A movement fires an action only when it crosses a set speed, angle or force.
mechanics.showsIt: Wii Sports (the swing's speed and timing set the shot)
mechanics.tryIt: Clap to act, but only claps loud enough to hear across the room count.
mechanics.buildIt: Measure a landmark's speed or a joint's angle each frame and fire when it crosses a threshold; the threshold is a number to tune.
mechanics.aiAngle: Where the threshold sits decides who can play: a tuning question about bodies.
mechanics.source: EG, after Marlon's Nov 17 10:47 note on MediaPipe and motion-to-result mechanics (via EL, format v1.5)
